A neighbor gave me my cat because she knew her. The cat stayed there for a week doing who knows what! They diagnosed a urinary tract infection! In short, the cat came back worse than before and died a week later. I asked the person who took the cat there for an invoice, and she refused and was even rude when I insisted we pay. A few days later they sent an invoice for the time the cat was there, just over 300 euros. My wife replied to the email asking for the payment details and reference number, but they never sent them, and now they're threatening lawyers when they themselves failed so badly with the animal that the diagnosis turned out to be a tumor, and they still haven't sent the payment information. The cat died because of their incompetence! Thieves…

I took my cat to this veterinary hospital several times, hoping they could resolve a gastric health problem she had.
I was almost always seen by Dr. Francisco, who has an unprofessional and overly casual attitude during consultations. However, I do not recommend the hospital due to treatment failures, namely:
1. He recommended a medication related to kidney problems based solely on blood tests. I later discovered, through different veterinarians, that the appropriate treatment would be a urine test, and only then should she take that medication. My cat had urine tests done at another hospital, where it was verified that taking the medication was unnecessary (therefore, the cat took daily medication unnecessarily and inappropriately).

2. He requested an ultrasound, but did not prescribe any sedative for the cat, even though I asked and explained that the cat gets too nervous in these situations, and that she had taken sedatives in the past without any adverse side effects. My cat underwent an ultrasound under a lot of unnecessary stress, affecting the work of the doctor who performed the exam. This same doctor (who had been selected by Dr. Francisco) told me that the cat should have been given a sedative beforehand, much to my frustration.

3. Finally, he suggested giving my cat a stomach protector and wrote the prescription. However, when I checked the prescription, I noticed that the dosage Dr. Francisco indicated for the cat was the same as an adult should take. When I checked the correct dosage for a cat myself, I found it should be 10 times lower than the one prescribed by Dr. Francisco. I called the clinic thinking it was a mistake, but Dr. Francisco insisted that I should give that huge dose (suitable for an adult) to a cat weighing less than 5 kg, justifying it by saying the cat would "spit out" a large part of the medication. I insisted to the doctor that this would be impossible, as the tablet in question was a capsule tablet, and therefore would be swallowed completely, making it impossible for a cat to spit out medication. I ended up opening the capsule and removing most of the powder, giving a reduced dose which, to no one's surprise, the cat swallowed completely without "spitting out" anything.
Given these completely inadequate treatments, I sought treatment for my cat at another hospital, and I recommend that potential future clients avoid this hospital.
